title: Pityriasis versicolor
summary: Malassezia yeast overgrowth causing pale, pink or brown finely scaly patches on the trunk. Treat with a ketoconazole wash and warn that the colour takes months to return.

glance.think: Well-defined pale, pink or fawn macules with fine, bran-like scale on the upper trunk and shoulders of a young adult, often noticed after a holiday.
glance.engine: Overgrowth of Malassezia, a normal skin yeast, in warm, sweaty, sebum-rich skin. It interferes with melanin production.
glance.backbone: Ketoconazole 2% shampoo used as a body wash for 5 days, or an azole cream for small areas.
glance.never_miss: Not dangerous. Make sure it is not vitiligo (no scale, depigmented) or pityriasis alba in children.

what: Pityriasis versicolor is a common, superficial yeast infection that causes **patchy colour change with fine scale**, usually on the trunk. It is caused by *Malassezia*, a yeast that is part of normal skin flora.
Because the organism is a normal skin resident, the condition is **not contagious in the usual sense**. It is an overgrowth rather than something caught.

list: Lipophilic *Malassezia* overgrows in sebum-rich skin (chest, back, shoulders, neck).
It produces substances that **interfere with melanin**, giving hypopigmented patches, or causes mild inflammation, giving pink or brown hyperpigmented patches.
**Promoters:** heat, humidity, sweating, oily skin and young adulthood. Mild immunosuppression can contribute.
Well-demarcated **hypopigmented, hyperpigmented or pink-fawn** macules that coalesce into patches.
**Fine, bran-like scale**, which becomes more obvious when the skin is gently scratched or stretched (the ‘evoked scale’ sign).
Sites: upper trunk, shoulders, neck and upper arms.
Usually asymptomatic or mildly itchy. Often noticed **after tanning**, because affected skin does not tan.
Skin scrapings or tape-stripping for microscopy show the classic **‘spaghetti and meatballs’** hyphae and spores.
Wood’s lamp may show a yellow-green fluorescence, but this is variable.

head: Look-alike
Distinguishing clues
rows: Complete depigmentation (chalk-white), **no scale**, often on the hands, face and around orifices
Children; ill-defined pale patches on the face, associated with atopy
History of a previous rash at the same sites; no scale
Greasy scale; scalp, face and central chest
Herald patch, then a ‘Christmas-tree’ pattern; self-limiting over 6–8 weeks

list: **Extensive:** **ketoconazole 2% shampoo** used as a body wash once daily for up to **5 days**. Lather onto the affected skin, leave for 3–5 minutes, then rinse. Licensed for this use from age 12.
**Small areas:** an azole (clotrimazole, econazole, ketoconazole) or terbinafine cream twice daily for 2–3 weeks. **Clotrimazole is preferred in pregnancy.**

management.h: If topicals fail or disease is very widespread

management: Oral **itraconazole** or **fluconazole** in adults. Check interactions and pregnancy status. Seek specialist advice for pregnancy or children.
Recurrence is common. Options are ketoconazole shampoo every 1–4 weeks, or a 3-day course before a sunny holiday.
red_flags: Diagnostic doubt, especially no scale or complete depigmentation (think vitiligo).
Very extensive, recurrent or unusual disease: consider immunosuppression.
Pregnancy or children needing oral therapy: seek specialist advice.
pearls: **Manage expectations:** the colour takes **weeks to months** to return after the yeast is cleared. This is **not** treatment failure.
Reassure that it is **not** caused by poor hygiene and is not usually catching.
Even sun exposure after treatment helps the colour even out. Ongoing scale suggests the infection is still active.
A prophylaxis plan before holidays prevents a lot of repeat consultations.
